newsitem.title: USA: NYC Council sees bigger revenues than mayor.
newsitem.headline: NYC Council sees bigger revenues than mayor.

text.p: New York City, which like New York State relies heavily on Wall Street's earnings, likely will get a big boost from the strength this sector has displayed for most of this year, the City Council has said.

The City Council, which enjoys a solid reputation for its revenue forecasts, sees an even bigger windfall for fiscal 1997, which ends on June 30, than the $50 million to $100 million estimate from the State Deputy Comptroller for New York City, Rosemary Scanlon. These extra funds would be on top of the $391 million forecast the state already expects the city to get.

"Our revenue projections are slightly higher than the comptrollers, both for the city and the state. So we think fiscal 1997 is better than being projected, and fiscal 1998 as well," Tom McMahon, the Council's director of finance, said on Friday.
New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi has forecast that the city's 1997 surplus would range from $220 million to $396 million. The city's 1997 fiscal year ends on June 30.

Projecting that Wall Street banks and brokerage houses will top the estimated $11.5 billion they earned in 1996, Gov George Pataki looks for the state to collect an extra $300 million by the time its 1997 fiscal year ends on March 31, boosting its surplus to a total of about $1.6 billion.
And from late February until the end of the 1998 fiscal year, he looks for New York State's revenues to surpass his initial estimates by around $650 million
